propositions.text: The appellants are appealing the Federal Court's summary trial judgment of February 24, 2022.
propositions.quote: The appellants, Vidéotron Ltée (Vidéotron) and Groupe TVA inc. (Groupe TVA), are appealing from the judgment by way of summary trial rendered by Justice Grammond of the Federal Court (the Judge) on February 24, 2022 (2022 FC 256).

propositions.text: The Judge held Konek and Hill Valley jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmission of Groupe TVA stations.
propositions.quote: the Judge held that the respondent companies, Technologies Konek inc. (Konek) and Coopérative de câblodistribution Hill Valley (Hill Valley), are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in the retransmission of Groupe TVA stations

propositions.text: The Judge exonerated Libéo from liability relating to the infringements at issue.
propositions.quote: the Judge exonerated the respondent company Libéo inc. (Libéo) from any liability relating to the infringements at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants appeal the Federal Court's summary judgment holding Konek and Hill Valley liable but exonerating Libéo.

propositions.text: Appellants ask this Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements due to direct involvement.
propositions.quote: the appellants are asking this Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for infringements of Groupe TVA’s copyright under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. (1985), c. C-42 (CA) because of its direct involvement in these infringements.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue Libéo should be held jointly liable for copyright infringements due to its direct involvement.

propositions.text: After reviewing the record and arguments, the Court would allow the appeal.
propositions.quote: Having carefully read the record and examined the oral and written arguments of the parties, I would allow the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it would allow the appeal after reviewing the record and arguments.

propositions.text: The Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17 of his decision, which are reproduced here as relevant.
propositions.quote: The Judge aptly summarized the facts of this case (Judge’s decision at paras. 8–17). It is therefore appropriate to reproduce the most relevant of these facts for the purposes of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17, which are reproduced here.

propositions.text: TVA Group is a Canadian broadcaster owning TVA and TVA Sports stations.
propositions.quote: The appellant TVA Group is a Canadian television broadcaster that owns and operates a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports.

propositions.text: Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) that retransmits TVA and TVA Sports stations to subscribers.
propositions.quote: The appellant Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) under the Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11. As a BDU, Vidéotron receives and retransmits a number of television stations to its subscribers, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states TVA Group owns TVA stations; Vidéotron is a BDU retransmitting these stations to subscribers.

propositions.text: Libéo, founded in 1996 by Rousseau, operates in IT and website hosting; Rousseau was CEO until 2019, Bussière president since 2016.
propositions.quote: The respondent Libéo, founded in 1996 (under the name Technologies Sys-Tech) by Jean-François Rousseau, is a company that operates in the information technology and website‑hosting field. Jean-François Rousseau was Libéo’s chief executive officer until 2019, and Joé Bussière has been its president since 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Libéo is an IT company founded by Rousseau, who was CEO until 2019; Bussière has been president since 2016.

propositions.text: In 2016, Rousseau partnered with Michaud to form Konek Technologies Inc. to design hotel technological solutions.
propositions.quote: In 2016, while he was Libéo’s chief executive officer, Jean-François Rousseau began a partnership with Louis Michaud to design new technological solutions for hotels. To that end, they formed Konek Technologies Inc.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau and Michaud formed Konek Technologies Inc. in 2016 to design hotel technology solutions.

propositions.text: In 2018, Konek designed the 'Konek box' under contract with Libéo, enabling hotel TVs to retransmit stations.
propositions.quote: A few years later, under a contract with Libéo in 2018, Konek designed a product known as the [translation] “Konek box”. This box allows televisions in hotel rooms to perform several functions, including retransmitting a number of television stations in hotel rooms.

propositions.text: Rousseau gradually disengaged from Libéo and left CEO position in 2019.
propositions.quote: In the years following the contract between Konek and Libéo, Jean-François Rousseau gradually disengaged from his responsibilities at Libéo and left his position as chief executive officer in 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Konek designed the 'Konek box' for Libéo in 2018; Rousseau left Libéo CEO role in 2019.

propositions.text: In February 2020, Rousseau helped form Hill Valley to provide more TV stations to hotels subscribing to Konek’s services.
propositions.quote: In February 2020, Jean-François Rousseau was involved in forming Hill Valley with the aim of providing a broader range of television stations to hotels subscribing to Konek’s services.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau helped form Hill Valley in 2020 to expand TV station offerings to hotels using Konek’s services.

propositions.text: Hill Valley applied to CRTC for BDU exemption on December 30, 2020; approved February 3, 2021.
propositions.quote: On December 30, 2020, Hill Valley applied to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to be recognized as a BDU exempt from the requirements of the Broadcasting Act while being subject to a more limited set of obligations. The CRTC approved Hill Valley’s application for exemption on February 3, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Hill Valley applied for and received CRTC BDU exemption between December 2020 and February 2021.

propositions.text: Vidéotron discovered Konek and Hill Valley retransmitting TVA stations via Internet in hotel rooms in 2020.
propositions.quote: Having become aware of Konek’s television station retransmission activities in 2020, Vidéotron ran various checks in hotel rooms served by Konek. The results of the checks performed by Vidéotron showed that Konek and Hill Valley were using the Internet to retransmit content, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations, to their subscribers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Vidéotron found Konek and Hill Valley retransmitting TVA stations via Internet in hotels in 2020.

propositions.text: On February 26, 2021, appellants sued Konek, Hill Valley, Libéo and their directors for copyright infringement.
propositions.quote: Therefore, on February 26, 2021, the appellants instituted proceedings in the Federal Court, alleging that Konek, Hill Valley and Libéo as well as their directing minds (Jean-François Rousseau, Joé Bussière and Louis Michaud) infringed TVA Group’s copyright by communicating to the public by telecommunication programs broadcast on the TVA and TVA Sports stations without authorization or without having previously obtained a licence for this purpose.

propositions.text: On same day, Vidéotron terminated service contract with Libéo for decoders used to retransmit TVA stations.
propositions.quote: On the same day, Vidéotron sent Libéo a notice of termination of the service contract between them for the decoders used to retransmit the feed from the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants sued Konek, Hill Valley, Libéo and directors for copyright infringement and terminated Libéo's service contract on February 26, 2021.

propositions.text: The Judge set out summary trial framework and agreed with parties to limit debate to corporate entities, excluding directors' liability.
propositions.quote: Before addressing the merits of the case, the Judge set out the framework for a summary trial and then agreed with the parties that it was appropriate in the circumstances to proceed by way of summary trial pursuant to rule 216 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106 (Tremblay v. Orio Canada Inc., 2013 FC 109, [2014] 3 F.C.R. 404 at para. 24). Before the Judge, the parties agreed that the issue of directors’ liability should not be decided at the summary trial and that the debate should therefore be limited to the corporate entities, namely, Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge framed the summary trial and limited issues to corporate entities, excluding directors' liability.

propositions.text: Appellants argued Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley infringed copyright by retransmitting TVA stations.
propositions.quote: The appellants (plaintiffs) therefore argued that the respondents Konek, Libéo and Hill Valley (defendants) had infringed their copyright by retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

propositions.text: Respondents argued retransmission was covered by section 31 exemption, so no infringement occurred.
propositions.quote: For their part, the respondents (defendants) replied that the said retransmission was covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA and that the appellants’ (plaintiffs’) copyright had therefore not been infringed.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argued infringement by retransmission; respondents claimed exemption under section 31 of the Copyright Act.

propositions.text: Judge found retransmission of TVA Sports not covered by section 31 exemption.
propositions.quote: The retransmission of TVA Sports is not covered by section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 45, 100).

propositions.text: Before February 3, 2021, Konek and Hill Valley did not qualify as 'retransmitters' under section 31 and could not claim exemption for TVA retransmission.
propositions.quote: Prior to February 3, 2021, neither Konek nor Hill Valley qualified as a “retransmitter” under section 31 of the CA. Therefore, they could not avail themselves of the exemption set out in the CA for the retransmission of TVA (Judge’s decision at paras. 53–54, 100).

propositions.text: Konek and Hill Valley are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmission not covered by section 31 exemption.
propositions.quote: Konek and Hill Valley are jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements committed by either corporation in the retransmission of the TVA and TVA Sports stations, where such retransmission is not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA (Judge’s decision at paras. 95, 101).

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found TVA Sports retransmission not exempt, Konek and Hill Valley not qualified as retransmitters before Feb 3, 2021, and liable for infringements.

propositions.text: Judge found Konek and Hill Valley jointly liable for copyright infringements not exempted by section 31.
propositions.quote: The Judge thus determined that two of the three corporate entities concerned, namely, Konek and Hill Valley, were jointly and severally liable for infringing the appellant TVA Group’s copyright when the retransmissions were not covered by the exemption set out in section 31 of the CA.

propositions.text: Judge found Libéo not liable for copyright infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley.
propositions.quote: However, he expressed the view that Libéo, the third corporate entity concerned, was not liable for the copyright infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations (Declaratory Judgment at paras. 4–5).

propositions.text: Appellants challenge the Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from copyright infringement liability.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, the appellants are challenging the Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from copyright infringements in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Konek and Hill Valley liable but exonerated Libéo; appellants challenge Libéo's exoneration.

propositions.text: Court allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the CA, but these are not at issue here.
propositions.quote: It should be noted that, during the hearing, this Court exceptionally allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on behalf of the respondents relating to subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the CA, even though Mr. Spicer did not appear on the record. Be that as it may, these subsections are not at issue in this appeal, and there is therefore no need to rule on their scope.

paragraphs.summary: The court allowed brief representations on subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the CA, but these are not at issue in this appeal.

propositions.text: Standard of review: correctness for questions of law; palpable and overriding error for fact or mixed fact and law (Housen v. Nikolaisen).
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review in this case is set out in Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 (Housen). The standard of correctness applies to questions of law (Housen at para. 8), but findings of fact or questions of mixed fact and law are reviewable only where the trial judge has made a palpable and overriding error (Housen at paras. 10, 36).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is correctness for law and palpable error for fact or mixed questions, per Housen v. Nikolaisen.

propositions.text: Issue: Did the Judge err in applying the legal principles and correctly identify the legal framework?
propositions.quote: This appeal raises the issue of whether the Judge erred in his application of the applicable legal principles. More specifically, did the Judge correctly identify the legal framework on which his analysis is based?

propositions.text: If trial judge uses wrong legal principle, no deference is owed (Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development)).
propositions.quote: as this Court recently mentioned in Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development), 2022 FCA 14, [2022] F.C.J. No. 72 (QL) at paragraph 109, “[i]f the trial judge conducts his analysis on the basis of the wrong legal principle, no deference is owed.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the Judge erred in legal framework application; no deference if wrong legal principle used.

propositions.text: It is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in Canada to many programs broadcast on TVA and TVA Sports stations.
propositions.quote: Although the Judge remained silent on the issue of ownership of rights, it is not disputed in this case that Groupe TVA owns the copyright in Canada to a wide variety of programs. Some of these programs are produced directly or through its subsidiary and are then broadcast on a number of television stations, including TVA and TVA Sports.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in Canada to programs broadcast on TVA and TVA Sports stations.

propositions.text: Subsection 3(1) of the CA grants Groupe TVA the sole right to communicate its programs by telecommunication.
propositions.quote: Thus, under subsection 3(1) of the CA, Groupe TVA has, among other things, the sole right to communicate Groupe TVA Programs to the public by telecommunication

paragraphs.summary: The court states that subsection 3(1) of the CA grants Groupe TVA the sole right to communicate its programs by telecommunication.

propositions.text: CCH states subsection 3(1) includes the right to authorize acts, and authorization can be inferred from acts or indifference.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court also discussed the issues involved in determining whether copyright infringement was authorized. It ruled that to authorize means to “[g]ive approval to; sanction, permit; favour, encourage” and that it can be inferred from acts or indifference

propositions.text: Authorization is a factual question depending on circumstances and can be inferred from less than direct acts including indifference.
propositions.quote: Authorization is a question of fact that depends on the circumstances of each particular case and can be inferred from acts that are less than direct and positive, including a sufficient degree of indifference.

propositions.text: Authorizing infringement is not established by authorizing mere use of equipment that could infringe copyright.
propositions.quote: However, a person does not authorize infringement by authorizing the mere use of equipment that could be used to infringe copyright.

propositions.text: Courts presume authorization is only for lawful activity.
propositions.quote: Courts should presume that a person who authorizes an activity does so only so far as it is in accordance with the law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CCH's legal principles on authorization of copyright infringement, including factual inquiry and presumption of lawful authorization.

propositions.text: The presumption of authorization may be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between authorizer and infringers.
propositions.quote: This presumption may be rebutted if it is shown that a certain relationship or degree of control existed between the alleged authorizer and the persons who committed the copyright infringement.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes CCH's statement that the presumption of authorization can be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between authorizer and infringers.

propositions.text: Sirius Canada says CCH does not require a particular legal relationship to rebut the presumption of authorization.
propositions.quote: this Court expressed the view that CCH did not “necessarily [require] a particular legal relationship between the user of equipment and the person authorizing its use” to rebut the presumption

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Sirius Canada that CCH does not require a particular legal relationship to rebut authorization presumption.

propositions.text: Paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA excludes from communication to the public those who only provide telecommunication means for others to communicate.
propositions.quote: a person whose only act in respect of the communication of a work or other subject-matter to the public consists of providing the means of telecommunication necessary for another person to so communicate the work or other subject-matter does not communicate that work or other subject-matter to the public

paragraphs.summary: The court states paragraph 2.4(1)(b) excludes from communication those who only provide telecommunication means for others to communicate.

propositions.text: SOCAN and Lackman hold that intermediaries acting as conduits without knowledge or influence are protected by paragraph 2.4(1)(b).
propositions.quote: an intermediary who is in fact merely acting as a “channel of communication”, has no knowledge of the content and allows others to communicate without influencing the content, will be considered a “conduit” and, as such, will benefit from the protection conferred by paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes SOCAN and Lackman that intermediaries acting as conduits without knowledge or influence are protected by paragraph 2.4(1)(b).

propositions.text: Paragraph 31.1(1) of the CA exempts providers of Internet or digital network services from copyright infringement solely for providing telecommunication or reproduction means.
propositions.quote: A person who, in providing services related to the operation of the Internet or another digital network, provides any means for the telecommunication or the reproduction of a work or other subject-matter through the Internet or that other network does not, solely by reason of providing those means, infringe copyright

paragraphs.summary: The court states paragraph 31.1(1) exempts providers of Internet or digital network services from copyright infringement solely for providing telecommunication means.

propositions.text: The Judge erred requiring proof of fraud, abuse of right or public order contravention to lift Libéo's corporate veil.
propositions.quote: The appellants submit that the Judge erred in finding that Libéo was not liable ... on the grounds that the appellants did not establish the “fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order”

propositions.text: Lifting the corporate veil was not an issue the Judge had to decide, so appellants did not have to establish it.
propositions.quote: The appellants allege that they did not have to establish this, as requested by the Judge, because lifting the corporate veil ... was not one of the issues that the Judge had to decide.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the Judge erred by requiring proof of fraud or abuse to lift Libéo's corporate veil, which was not an issue before him.

propositions.text: Libéo argues the Judge did not err given the evidence at summary trial.
propositions.quote: the respondent Libéo essentially argues that, given the evidence submitted to the Judge at the summary trial, he did not commit a palpable and overriding error

propositions.text: Respondents criticize the Judge for ruling on issues not submitted, including Hill Valley's BDU qualification and unspecified periods.
propositions.quote: they also criticize the Judge for ruling on issues that were not submitted to him by the parties ... did not have to rule on the periods that had not been specified

propositions.text: No cross-appeal was filed on the issue of Hill Valley's BDU status, so the Court will not address it.
propositions.quote: since no cross-appeal was filed, the issue is not before us, and there is therefore no need for this Court to address it.

paragraphs.summary: Libéo argues the Judge did not err and criticizes ruling on unsubmitted issues; the Court declines to address Hill Valley's BDU status due to no cross-appeal.

propositions.text: Appellants insist lifting Libéo's corporate veil was not submitted to the Judge and they did not have to establish it.
propositions.quote: the appellants insisted that the issue of lifting Libéo’s corporate veil had not been submitted to the Judge. They allege that they did not have to establish this

propositions.text: Libéo concedes appellants did not refer to corporate veil but says Judge applied it because appellants argued companies were inseparable.
propositions.quote: Libéo concedes that the appellants did not refer to the corporate veil but asserts that the Judge applied the principle because the appellants argued that the companies were intrinsically linked or inseparable.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants say corporate veil was not submitted; Libéo concedes but says Judge applied it due to appellants' inseparability argument.

propositions.text: Parties' memoranda confirm corporate veil was not raised; Judge understood appellants claimed Konek and Hill Valley were one and Libéo liable for leasing decoders.
propositions.quote: The parties’ memoranda at trial confirm that the corporate veil was not an issue raised by the parties. The Judge also seemed to have understood the position of the appellants ... The plaintiffs essentially contend that Konek and Hill Valley are one and the same. They also claim that Libéo is liable because it leased from Vidéotron decoders

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties did not raise corporate veil; Judge understood appellants claimed Konek and Hill Valley were one and Libéo liable for leasing decoders.

propositions.text: Judge examined lifting corporate veil and ruled Libéo not liable as facts did not allow overriding separate legal personalities.
propositions.quote: The fact that the same people are shareholders or directors of Konek and Libéo does not override the separate legal personalities of these corporations ... it is only in cases of fraud, abuse of right or contravention of a rule of public order that the corporate veil is lifted ... The plaintiffs proved no such thing.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Libéo not liable, ruling facts did not justify lifting the corporate veil absent fraud or abuse.

propositions.text: Appellants did not allege Libéo liable via lifting corporate veil but for direct copyright infringement by telecommunication.
propositions.quote: the appellants did not allege at trial that Libéo should be held liable for Konek and Hill Valley’s faults ... Rather, the appellants alleged that Libéo was liable for copyright infringements for having directly communicated Groupe TVA’s programs by telecommunication

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants alleged Libéo liable for direct copyright infringement, not via lifting the corporate veil.

propositions.text: Judge applied incorrect legal framework focusing on lifting corporate veil and fault of another, not Libéo's direct fault.
propositions.quote: the Judge’s analysis necessarily focused on the issue of Libéo’s liability through the lens of the fault of another ... while it was Libéo’s direct fault that was at issue ... the Judge therefore applied an incorrect legal framework

propositions.text: Judge should have asked parties for submissions if concerned about corporate veil but did not, so had to decide on record and arguments submitted.
propositions.quote: if the Judge was concerned about the corporate veil issue, he had to ask the parties to make submissions on this matter and, if necessary, additional representations ... he was required to decide all the issues on the basis of the record and the arguments submitted to him

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Judge applied the wrong legal framework and should have sought submissions if concerned about corporate veil.

propositions.text: Had the Judge used correct legal framework, he would have found Libéo liable for copyright infringement.
propositions.quote: had the Judge based his analysis on the appropriate legal framework, I am of the view that ... he would have had to find Libéo liable for infringing Groupe TVA’s copyright

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes that with the correct legal framework, the Judge would have found Libéo liable for copyright infringement.

propositions.text: Judge relied on Rousseau's and Bussière's testimony to find Libéo not liable for copyright infringement.
propositions.quote: The Judge also accepted Joé Bussière’s testimony that he was unaware of the existence of Vidéotron’s decoders ... Libéo is therefore not liable for any copyright infringements committed by Konek or Hill Valley.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Libéo not liable based on Rousseau's and Bussière's testimony about decoders and lack of awareness.

propositions.text: All evidence contradicts the Judge’s finding when analyzed under correct legal framework.
propositions.quote: all the evidence in the record, analyzed within the correct legal framework, contradicts the Judge’s finding

paragraphs.summary: The court finds all evidence contradicts the Judge's finding under the correct legal framework.

propositions.text: Rousseau and Bussière have long business relationship with overlapping roles in Libéo and Konek.
propositions.quote: Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière have a long-standing business relationship and collaborate in various information technology companies ... they hold important overlapping roles within Libéo and Konek

propositions.text: Rousseau founded Libéo, was president and CEO, remains majority shareholder with ultimate control; Bussière replaced him as president and is second largest shareholder.
propositions.quote: Jean-François Rousseau founded Libéo ... He was its president until 2016 and its chief executive officer until March 2019 ... He still remains Libéo’s majority shareholder with “ultimate control” ... Joé Bussière replaced Jean-François Rousseau as president of Libéo in 2016 and remains its second largest shareholder

propositions.text: Libéo is a small business with two directors: Rousseau and Bussière.
propositions.quote: It appears that Libéo is a small business composed of two directors: Jean-François Rousseau and Joé Bussière

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rousseau and Bussière have overlapping roles and control in Libéo and Konek, with Libéo a small business of two directors.

propositions.text: Konek was co-founded by Bussière and Rousseau, who are equal shareholders and directors.
propositions.quote: Konek was co-founded by Joé Bussière and Jean-François Rousseau. Mr. Bussière is a director and equal shareholder with Jean-François Rousseau

propositions.text: Konek provides TV and internet services for hotels, including TVA and TVA Sports channels.
propositions.quote: Konek provides integrated TV, IP telephony, Internet and Wi-Fi services for hotels ... provide access to a large number of live television stations, including the TVA and TVA Sports stations

propositions.text: Konek shared premises with Libéo until Sept 2019, then located next door.
propositions.quote: Since its founding until September 2019, Konek shared the same premises as Libéo ... Since September 2019, Konek has been located next to Libéo

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Konek was co-founded by Bussière and Rousseau, provides TV services including TVA channels, and shared premises with Libéo until 2019.

propositions.text: Libéo played important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure including encoding servers.
propositions.quote: After entering into a contract with Konek in 2018, Libéo played an important role in Konek ... Libéo knew that Konek was going to provide its television services using its infrastructure, including encoding capture servers

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Libéo played an important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure including encoding servers.

propositions.text: Libéo was involved in developing Konek's infrastructure, enabling customer access to Konek services.
propositions.quote: after signing the contract, Libéo was involved in developing several aspects of Konek’s infrastructure, in turn allowing Konek’s customers to have access to Konek services.

propositions.text: Libéo designed and supplied 'Konek boxes'.
propositions.quote: designing and supplying “Konek boxes” (Judge’s decision at para. 10)

propositions.text: Libéo developed software for the Konek boxes.
propositions.quote: developing software for the boxes (Judge’s decision at para. 96)

propositions.text: Libéo provided infrastructure and servers, including encoding capture servers for TV content, to operate Konek services.
propositions.quote: providing the infrastructure and servers needed to operate Konek services, including “encoding capture servers” for television content (Judge’s decision at paras. 96, 99 and Appeal Book, tab 26 at 64–66).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Libéo developed Konek's infrastructure, designed boxes, developed software, and provided servers for Konek services.

propositions.text: Joé Bussière confirmed Vidéotron technician accessed Libéo's secure room during ILLICO decoder installation.
propositions.quote: Joé Bussière confirmed that, when the ILLICO decoders were being installed, a Vidéotron technician had access to Libéo’s secure room

propositions.text: A Libéo director knew the server room contained ILLICO terminals.
propositions.quote: a Libéo director knew that the server room contained ILLICO terminals

propositions.text: Jean-François Rousseau personally gave Vidéotron technician access to Libéo server room and still had access as of Sept 27, 2021.
propositions.quote: Jean-François Rousseau confirmed that he had personally given the Vidéotron technician access to the Libéo server room because he himself had access to it. He further confirmed that, as of the date of his cross-examination, September 27, 2021, he still had access to Libéo’s server room.

paragraphs.summary: Witnesses confirmed Vidéotron technician accessed Libéo's server room containing ILLICO terminals, with Rousseau personally granting access and retaining it.

propositions.text: Some ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were tuned to TVA Sports and retransmitted to hotels.
propositions.quote: some of the ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were constantly tuned to TVA Group’s TVA Sports station and then retransmitted to hotels

propositions.text: Respondents claim Konek paid for ILLICO decoders, so Libéo did not retransmit TVA content and is not liable.
propositions.quote: it was Konek who paid for them directly, and Libéo “is therefore not the one who retransmitted the TVA and TVA Sports content” and, consequently, was not liable

propositions.text: This argument is without merit; Libéo was responsible for use of rented ILLICO decoders on its premises.
propositions.quote: This argument is without merit. As a contracting entity for the rental of the ILLICO decoders, Libéo was responsible for the way it used these decoders, located on its premises.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue Libéo not liable as Konek paid for decoders, but court rejects this, holding Libéo responsible for decoder use on its premises.

propositions.text: A Libéo website document describes a partnership and alliance with Konek, highlighting Libéo's innovation role in Konek.ai's success.
propositions.quote: The screenshot, entitled “100% made at Libéo”, also describes the relationship between Libéo and Konek as one of “partnership” and “alliance” and indicates that “Libéo’s innovation skills are at the heart of Konek.ai’s success”.

paragraphs.summary: A Libéo website document evidences a partnership and alliance with Konek, emphasizing Libéo's innovation in Konek.ai's success.

propositions.text: Given evidence of close ties, it is difficult to find Libéo unaware of decoder use and not actively participating in retransmitting TVA content.
propositions.quote: it is extremely difficult to find that “there is no evidence that Libéo was aware of the specific use” of the decoders and that therefore it did not actively participate in communicating TVA Group’s Programs by telecommunication.

propositions.text: Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron services via ILLICO decoders, receiving and illegally retransmitting TVA signals through Konek's services.
propositions.quote: Libéo has subscribed to Vidéotron’s television services through the rental of the ILLICO decoders. It therefore receives the signal, including the Groupe TVA stations, and retransmits it illegally through Konek’s services.

propositions.text: Libéo is directly participating and cannot claim exemptions under the Copyright Act.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the evidence has established Libéo’s direct participation, and Libéo is therefore not in a position to avail itself of the exemptions set out in the CA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Libéo directly participated in illegal retransmission of TVA content and cannot claim Copyright Act exemptions.

propositions.text: Appellants submit Judge erred by not ordering permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley after finding section 31 CA did not apply.
propositions.quote: the appellants submit that, given the Judge’s finding that section 31 of the CA did not apply, the Judge should have ordered a permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley

propositions.text: Appellants argue Judge erred in law by relying on too narrow a view of judicial contract to refuse injunction.
propositions.quote: he erred in law by relying on too narrow a view of the judicial contract to justify his refusal.

propositions.text: Appellants do not ask Court to decide injunction issue as separate ground but to address it obiter due to unclear case law on summary trials.
propositions.quote: The appellants are not asking this Court to decide this issue as a separate ground of appeal, but to address it in obiter because “there is little case law on the scope of summary trials, and the distinction is not always clear between the concepts of a preliminary determination of a point of law, a motion for a summary judgment and a motion for a summary trial”

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Judge erred by not ordering injunction and ask Court to address issue obiter due to unclear summary trial case law.

propositions.text: Court declines to address injunction issue abstractly as it was resubmitted to Judge at trial for fuller analysis.
propositions.quote: I do not find it appropriate for this Court to address this issue in the abstract, as the appellants would like, especially since the parties confirmed at the hearing that the injunction issue was resubmitted to the Judge at trial.

propositions.text: Judge found Konek and Hill Valley jointly liable for copyright infringements but declined injunction due to summary trial agreement scope.
propositions.quote: the Judge held that Konek and Hill Valley were jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements under the CA, but on the other hand he declined to rule on the injunction to end the infringement on the basis of the agreement between the parties regarding the scope of the motion for a summary trial

propositions.text: Appellants face summary judgment without practical effect, needing further proceedings and costs, contrary to proportionality and sound justice administration.
propositions.quote: Faced with a summary judgment without practical effect, the appellants have paradoxically found themselves in the same situation they were in prior to the summary trial despite a finding of copyright infringements and will have to institute further proceedings and incur further costs to have this issue decided at a later date. On its face, this result appears to run counter to proportionality and the sound administration of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Court declines to address injunction issue now; notes appellants face ineffective summary judgment and further costs, contrary to justice principles.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed; judgment set aside in part with costs; Libéo declared liable for copyright infringements and jointly liable with Konek and Hill Valley.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal, set aside the judgment in part, with costs, and render the judgment that the Federal Court judge should have rendered, namely, to declare Libéo liable for the copyright infringements through its direct participation in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations and jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements committed in retransmitting the TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows appeal, sets aside judgment in part, declares Libéo liable and jointly liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements.
